interactionPlan.concept: Endpoint Error (EPE) measures the accuracy of optical flow estimation by calculating the Euclidean distance between the ground truth and estimated flow vectors.
learningObjectives: Understand that optical flow displacement is a 2D vector with both magnitude (speed) and direction
Explain how Endpoint Error (EPE) geometrically represents the distance between the tips of the true and estimated vectors
Identify how independent errors in vector magnitude and vector angle combine to produce the total endpoint error
interactionPlan.keyInsight: Endpoint error is a single scalar metric that elegantly captures mismatches in both speed and direction as the straight-line distance between vector endpoints.

interactions.label: Estimation Angle
interactions.effect: Rotates the estimated vector (u-hat, v-hat) relative to the fixed ground-truth vector (u, v).
interactions.teaches: How directional mismatch alone creates endpoint error, even if the estimated speed is accurate.

interactions.label: Estimation Speed
interactions.effect: Scales the length (magnitude) of the estimated vector (u-hat, v-hat).
interactions.teaches: How underestimating or overestimating motion speed contributes to endpoint error.

demo_steps.title: Understanding the Vector Gap
demo_steps.narration: Look at the two vectors originating from the same point: the black vector represents the true motion (ground truth), and the blue vector represents our estimation. The red line connecting their endpoints is the Endpoint Error (EPE). Right now, because our estimation is both too short and pointing in the wrong direction, there is a visible gap between their endpoints.
demo_steps.focus: The red line (Endpoint Error) spanning the gap between the tips of the two vectors.

demo_steps.title: Isolating Speed Errors
demo_steps.narration: Align the direction of your estimate perfectly with the ground truth by setting the angle to 0, but keep the speed too high (1.5x). Notice that the endpoint error is now lying directly along the path of the vectors. This shows that even with perfect direction, a speed mismatch alone produces an endpoint error equal to the difference in their lengths.
demo_steps.focus: The red line segment lying flat along the overlapping vector lines.

demo_steps.title: Isolating Directional Drift
demo_steps.narration: Now, set the speed multiplier to exactly 1.0 so that the estimate has the correct magnitude, but rotate the angle to 45 degrees. Even though your algorithm correctly predicted the speed of the pixel, the directional drift creates a substantial endpoint error, forming an isosceles triangle.
demo_steps.focus: The base of the triangle formed by the red error line, connecting two vectors of equal length.

demo_steps.title: Achieving Perfect Estimation
demo_steps.narration: Align both controls perfectly with the ground truth (angle 0, speed multiplier 1.0). As the estimated vector matches the ground truth vector, the red error line shrinks to zero. This represents a perfect optical flow estimation where the endpoint error is zero.
demo_steps.focus: The complete collapse of the red error line as the two vectors perfectly overlap.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: The visualization should display two vectors starting from a shared origin at the bottom-left. One vector, representing ground truth (u, v), is static and colored solid black. The second vector, representing the estimate (u-hat, v-hat), is dynamic (colored blue) and changes based on the sliders. A prominent red line segment connects the arrowheads of both vectors, labeled 'Endpoint error (EPE)'. Dynamic text should display the calculated mathematical EPE value (e.g., 'EPE = 1.42 pixels') to give immediate quantitative feedback as the user interacts with the sliders.
